To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) higher order intentionality tasks require more time and more neurons than factual memory tasks; 2) higher orders of intentionality require more time and neurons than lower orders of intentionality; 3) the time and neurons required for intentionality are disproportionately more than those for factual memory; and 4) intentionality is cognitively more difficult than factual memory.

higher order intentionality tasks (i.e., those requiring participants to infer a character’s beliefs about a third character’s beliefs) are cognitively and neurally more demanding than lower order intentionality tasks.
higher orders of intentionality require more neurons in brain areas that are known to be associated to theory of mind and are disproportionately more demanding.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how we understand other people.
the cognitive demands of mentalising, and the implications that this has for models of brain and brain evolution.
the evolution of human cognition, in particular the development of the ability to think about the thoughts and feelings of others.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
social cognition is cognitively demanding, but that the demand is not uniform across different levels of social cognition.
mentalising is cognitively demanding, and that this demand increases as the order of mentalising increases.
social cognition is not cognitively more difficult than other cognitive processes, and that the brain does not have to work harder to perform social cognitive tasks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the cognitive demands of mentalising are higher than previously assumed, that these higher cognitive demands are reflected in the brain in terms of the time taken for responses and the recruitment of additional neurons and that these findings have implications for the evolution of the brain and social cognition.
social cognition is cognitively more costly, in terms of time, than non-social cognition, and the higher order the cognition, the more costly it is.
higher-order intentionality tasks are disproportionately more demanding, requiring longer reaction times and more neurons than lower order tasks.
The main takeaway from our work is that
social cognition may have been cognitively more costly than other types of cognition.
higher order intentionality tasks require more cognitive resources.
the brain regions that are involved in social cognition are also involved in the processing of other types of information.
